content: The field of organic chemistry is dedicated to the study of organic compounds. These compounds represent a vast array of chemicals, accounting for more than half of all known chemical compounds. To manage this extensive diversity, classification systems have been developed based on the functional groups present in the molecules. Examples of these classes include acid anhydrides, acyl halides, alcohols, aldehydes, alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, amides, amines, aromatics, azo compounds, carboxylic acids, esters, ethers, haloalkanes, imines, ketones, nitriles, nitro compounds, organometallic compounds, phenols, polymers (including all plastics), and thiols. Organic compounds also play a critical role in biochemistry. Key examples include antigens, polysaccharides, carbohydrates, sugars, enzymes, hormones, lipids, fatty acids, neurotransmitters, nucleic acids, proteins, peptides, amino acids, and vitamins. The term organic has historical roots dating back to the 19th century. At that time, it was believed that organic compounds could only be synthesized by living organisms through a life force known as vis vitalis. This theory was disproven when Friedrich Wöhler synthesized urea, an organic compound previously thought to occur only in the urine of living organisms, from inorganic precursors such as potassium cyanate and ammonium sulfate. This landmark achievement, known as the Wöhler synthesis, demonstrated that organic compounds could be produced from non-living sources, such as minerals. Today, most pure organic compounds are synthesized artificially. However, certain compounds are still extracted from natural sources because their artificial production would be prohibitively expensive. Examples include many sugars, some alkaloids, terpenoids, certain nutrients like vitamin B12, and other natural products with large or stereochemically complex molecules that are found in significant concentrations in living organisms. The statistical analysis of chemical structures is referred to as chemical informatics. The Beilstein database is a comprehensive repository of organic compounds, containing approximately six million molecules. Within this network, around two million molecules form a core structure resembling the interconnected nature of the World Wide Web. Interestingly, only 5% of these molecules are involved in 35% of all chemical reactions, which in turn give rise to 60% of all known molecules. Most synthetic pathways involve fewer than four steps, and 95% of all connecting reactions require fewer than 15 steps. Any molecule on the periphery of this network can typically be reached from the core in fewer than three steps. The relative size of the core of organic compounds peaked in 1880 and has since declined. However, the core still contains 70% of the top 200 industrial chemicals. This core includes two million organic compounds and features key reagents such as 10 Wittig reagents, six Grignard reagents, two DNA building blocks, and 18 aromatic aldehydes.
